note:
The introduction to the book, with v. 1 as the title, vv. 2–6 as the purpose, and v. 7 as the theme.

**1:1 proverbs.** The Hb. word translated as “proverb” has a range of meanings, but it is usually applied to an aphorism or maxim in a wisdom context. The prologue (1:1–7) applies to the whole book and the variety of wisdom sayings it contains, all broadly classified as “proverbs.”

**Solomon.** Although Solomon wrote many proverbs (1 Kin. 4:32), the words of sages other than Solomon are included under this heading (e.g., Agur, 30:1; and Lemuel, 31:1). Even in the materials attributed to Solomon, something other than direct authorship may at times be involved. Note that the “words of King Lemuel” were not authored by Lemuel but taught to him by his mother and then associated with Lemuel. So, too, at least some of the “proverbs of Solomon” could have been taught to him by others and then associated with him as Israel’s quintessential wise man. The roots of proverbial traditions in folk experience make it unlikely that Solomon was the exclusive originator of all the proverbs he put into writing (Introduction: Author).

**king.** Wisdom was a royal enterprise in the ancient Near East. The queen of Sheba came to listen to Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kin. 10:1) and the “men of Hezekiah king of Judah” copied some of the proverbs (Prov. 25:1).

Explicit reference to the purpose behind this collection suggests that some kind of formal educational use was being made of such materi­al, although evidence for wisdom schools (groups gathered around prominent teachers) in Israel is not strong.

**1:2 wisdom.** The purpose of Proverbs is to guide the reader into wisdom, a word with many nuances. It refers fundamentally to living in keeping with the order that God built into the world so as to survive and thrive. James 3:15–18 distinguishes heavenly wisdom from earthly wisdom; the former is defined very much in terms of the fruit of the Holy Spirit, while the latter is the opposite.

**instruction.** The word suggests moral and intellectual discipline. It often means the learning of wisdom.

**insight.** Or discernment, the ability to read between the lines and make correct distinctions.

These words can be used in religious and ethical contexts as well as in temporal affairs. At times, biblical wisdom shows concern with worldly matters, but it always does so within the framework of divine design in the created order.

Sound judgment.

**simple.** The word is paralleled in this verse by “youth”; it refers to those who are untutored, inexperienced, and easily deceived (1:10), not to those lacking intellectual powers. Wisdom is a matter of practical godliness.

**discretion.** The word suggests making right decisions with understanding.

Wisdom was institutionalized in the ancient culture in that the wise called upon people to improve their wisdom. Succeeding generations were to learn from those who went before (v. 8). Note the typical parallel structure of this verse in which almost synonymous phrases are joined.

**guidance.** This Hb. word, used only in Proverbs and Job, highlights the importance of right thinking and experience in decision making.

These different words may be used synonymously, as in Hab. 2:6, but probably here they are distinct forms of wisdom sayings, having as a common characteristic an enigma that challenges the intellect (1:1 note).

**saying.** Sometimes rendered “parable.” The parables of Jesus are somewhat different from what is found in the book of Proverbs, although they show the influence of Wisdom Literature.

**riddles.** Probably a broad but identifiable type of wisdom literature. The word is used of Samson’s riddle (Judg. 14:12–19), of an allegory (Ezek. 17:2), and of the sayings used to test Solomon (1 Kin. 10:1).

LORD**.** The main theme of Proverbs and ancient Israel’s decisive contribution to the human quest for knowledge and understanding. The fear of the Lord is the only basis of true knowledge. This fear is not distrustful terror of God but rather the reverent awe and worshipful response of faith to the God who reveals Himself as the Creator, the Savior, and the Judge.

Although Israel’s covenant relationship with God receives little overt attention in Proverbs, the use of the divine name most closely associated with the covenant, “Lord” (Hb. _Yahweh_; cf. Ex. 3:15; 6:3 and notes), is significant. It indicates that God’s redemptive covenant with His people and the special revelation that accompany it are foundational for true wisdom. In Deuteronomy, “fear the Lord” means living by the stipulations of the covenant in grateful response to God’s redemptive grace (Deut. 6:2, 24). The temple built by Solomon later became the visible expression of Israel’s covenant relationship with the Lord, which again is described as the “fear” of the Lord (1 Kin. 8:40, 43). There is an important link through Solomon and the temple between biblical wisdom and the covenant theology found elsewhere in the OT.

**is the beginning of knowledge.** See also 2:4–6; 9:10; 15:33; Job 28:28; Ps. 111:10. The Hebrew means either the starting point of knowledge or its best part. The former is in view here, not as in a starting point that one leaves behind, but as in mathematics, where one uses the numbers learned at the beginning in all of the later courses. While in His common grace God enables unbelievers to know much about the world, only the fear of the Lord enables one to know what anything means ultimately. Relying on this light, wisdom pursues the task of reflecting on human experience.

The first collection of proverbs in the book. It consists of longer poems that have as their primary function admonishing the youth mentioned in 1:4 to choose the way of wisdom.

**1:8–19** The first instructional poem, wherein the parents call the son to avoid the wrong path.

**1:8, 9** The instruction form of ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature typically begins with a call for attentiveness. Father and mother were both involved in home instruction.

**1:8 instruction.** See note on 3:1.

**teaching.** Hb. _torah_ in Proverbs refers mostly to human teaching (3:1; 4:2; 6:20, 23; 7:2; 13:14; 31:26). Four times _torah_ echoes divine instruction (28:4, 7, 9; 29:18) and is translated “law.” The human instruction in the book is at the same time divine instruction.
These metaphors portray the effect of wisdom: the garland is a symbol of victory (4:9) and the pendants are a symbol of luxury (Judg. 8:26).

Summarizes the instruction. The “if” will be expanded in vv. 11–14 and the “do not” in vv. 15–18. “If ... then” clauses are common throughout the book (see 2:4, 5).

**entice.** The Hb. verb is related to the noun translated “simple” in 1:4. The simple are easily enticed.

The realm of death is here depicted as ready to swallow its victims. Elsewhere, this poetic term denotes a realm where corruption is father and the worm is mother (Job 17:13, 14), a domain with gates (Is. 38:10). It is a land of no return (Job 7:9), silence (Ps. 94:17), darkness (Ps. 143:3), and forgetfulness (Ps. 88:11, 12). See notes on 9:18 and Is. 14:9–11.
Proverbs does not forbid or discourage wealth—only the use of evil to get it. However, the ultimate wealth is wisdom itself (2:4; 3:13–16; cf. Job 28:12–19).
After the extended conditional clause (vv. 10–14), the address is repeated to reinforce the command to avoid evil people.
This verse is almost identical with Is. 59:7 and is partly quoted by Paul in Rom. 3:15 as part of his demonstration that all are sinners.

This saying is introduced to strengthen the reasons for the author’s counsel. The apparent meaning is that even a bird will avoid a trap once it has knowledge of it. Those who are tempted should do the same.
One reaps what one sows. These “lie in wait” and plan to “ambush” others (v. 11), not knowing that they “lie in wait for their own blood” and “set an ambush for their own lives.”

Such folly is contrary to the true order of the world, which, though fallen, is still under God’s sovereign rule. This expression of inevitable retribution is based on the observable order of causes and consequence. Apparent interruptions in this pattern prompted other biblical writers to address the problem of the prosperous wicked and the suffering righteous (Job 1–42; Ps. 73).

These verses make up the first wisdom poem in the opening collection and focus on wisdom’s rebuke of the simple, with vv. 20, 21 as the setting, vv. 22–27 as the sermon, and vv. 28–33 as the significance.

**1:20** Wisdom is portrayed as an open-air preacher similar to the caller in Is. 55. Personified as a woman, she calls on the simple to repent of folly and to seek wisdom before it is too late. Personification of wisdom is found also in 3:14–18; 8:1–36; 9:1–12.

The town gate was the public forum for counsel and judgment (Deut. 22:15; 25:7; Ruth 4:1, 11; 2 Sam. 19:8). It is the place where the elders of the town often met. This is the fitting location for the figure of wisdom to call people to heed her counsel.

See v. 4 and note. There has been a development of thought. At issue is not merely gaining more insight but a deliberate choice between two ways. Wisdom and folly, righteousness and wickedness, are constantly opposed in Proverbs as the only two options for life (cf. Matt. 7:24–27).

**scoffers.** The precise meaning of this word, used mostly in Proverbs, is difficult to determine. The mocker (or scoffer) is a person who resists the discipline of the wise (9:7, 8; 13:1; 14:6; 21:11; Ps. 1).

**fools.** Unteachable people.

**knowledge.** See 1:7. In Wisdom Literature, “knowledge” is often a synonym for wisdom.

Proverbs recognizes wisdom as both a divine gift and a human task. The former is seen in 1:7, where the fear of the Lord grows from the grace of God in redemption. Redemption involves renewal of the mind as well as regeneration of the soul (Rom. 12:1, 2; 1 Cor. 1:18–2:6).
The rejection of wisdom’s message has its parallels in the rejection of God’s grace by Israel.
Here wisdom speaks with full authority. As God’s counsel, her counsel and advice are not open to debate (2:6; 8:14).
“He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (Ps. 2:4).
Storm imagery is frequent for divine judgment in the OT (e.g., Jer. 23:19; Jon. 1:9–12).

True wisdom is an aspect of God’s saving grace, and there comes a point of no return for those who reject it. This truth reinforces the urgency of the message. No one can expect God’s favor and at the same time scorn the gifts He offers (Deut. 1:45; 1 Sam. 28:6; Ps. 18:41).

A synonym for wisdom, explained here by the phrase parallel with it, “the fear of the LORD” (1:7 note). Wisdom comes from above (James 3:17) as God’s gift in redemptive revelation. This is true even when it must be desired and strived for (2:4–6; Heb. 5:7, 8; James 1:5).
The relationship between deed and outcome is observable in natural cause and effect. Here the image is not one of pleasure after a full meal but of disgust at being glutted.

Indifference or willful neglect.

**complacency of fools.** The ignorant self-satisfaction of the willfully unteachable, who see no need to learn anything from anyone.
This verse stands in direct contrast with v. 32. Wisdom brings life and security. To embrace wisdom is to embrace all that promotes life.

The second instructional poem of the first collection, with a focus on how wisdom will keep one safe. The poem is an acrostic, with vv. 1–11 governed by _aleph_ (the first letter of the first half of the Hebrew alphabet) and vv. 12–22 governed by _lamed_ (the first letter of the second half of the Hebrew alphabet). The _aleph_ stanza is divided into three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry), each beginning with a word that starts with _aleph_: “if” (vv. 1–4), “then” (vv. 5–8), and “then” (vv. 9–11). The _lamed_ stanza is also divided into three strophes, each beginning with a word that starts with _lamed_: “delivering ... from” (vv. 12–15), “delivered from” (vv. 16–19), and “So you will walk” (vv. 20–22).

**2:1–11** The development of wisdom.

**2:1–4** The conditions for developing wisdom.

**2:1 receive.** The first condition is the acceptance of wisdom (1:3).

**treasure.** The Hb. word has the sense of hiding something of value so as to protect it, and the means of hiding is memorization (Ps. 119:11).

The second condition is submission. To stretch out the heart is to submit. In Josh. 24:23 and 1 Kin. 11:2–4, such submission is a human responsibility, whereas in 1 Kin. 8:58 and Ps. 119:36, it is a matter of divine sovereignty. The heart is the seat of reason and the will. Today’s popular distinction between heart knowledge and head knowledge does not apply here. The usual OT contrast is between a formal or outward compliance lacking true assent of will and a willing, wholehearted compliance.
The third condition is humility. As wisdom called out (1:21) and raised her voice (1:20), humility responds in kind.

The fourth condition is desire. “Seek” and “silver” are rather common terms in the Hebrew Bible, but “search” and “hidden treasure” are rare. The movement from the common to the rare underscores the need for deep desire if one is going to develop wisdom.

**hidden treasures.** Note the similar image used by Jesus in Matt. 13:44.

The first result of meeting the conditions is wisdom in one’s relationship with God.

**2:5 you will understand ... knowledge.** Wisdom starts with the knowledge of God.

No matter how much we are engaged in the task of searching for knowledge through our human experience in the world, the source of all wisdom is God (Job 28). He must provide the wisdom necessary for the proper interpretation of reality (3:5).

**from his mouth.** Although their emphasis is different, both Deuteronomy and Proverbs recognize that the underlying foundation of knowledge is the Word of God (Deut. 8:3). Even before sin had entered the world, Adam and Eve needed God’s revelation in order to know themselves and their relationship to creation (Gen. 1:28–30).
The character of God, which the wise come to know (v. 5), is the basis of morality. Standards of integrity and righteousness are expressions of wisdom.
People who show that they possess the fear of the Lord by imitating His covenant love.

The second result of meeting the conditions is wisdom in one’s relationship with others.

**2:9 righteousness and justice and equity.** Terms that articulate what should govern how we treat others.

**every good path.** The Wisdom Literature is important to our understanding of God’s guidance of our lives. It points to the task of gaining wisdom so we can make decisions that are responsible and consistent with our covenant status as God’s people (1 Pet. 2:9).
Resourcefulness or prudence.

The deliverance by wisdom.

**2:12–15.** Deliverance from evil men, from their evil speech and apostasy.

**2:12 evil.** The Hb. word is masculine and refers to evil men, not to evil in general, as is made clear by the word “men” in the second half of the verse.

**perverted speech.** Words of rebellion that overturn truth. Later proverbs will have much to say about speech.
The evil men turn away from the right path (see v. 17).

Deliverance from evil women, from their evil speech and apostasy.

**2:16 forbidden woman.** Adultery is a radical departure from God’s order for human relationships (5:1–23; 6:20–29; 7:1–27). The Hb. term is “foreign” or “strange” woman. In this context, it means a woman who is foreign to the proper marital relationship, a harlot or adulteress.

**smooth words.** As evil men use perverted speech (v. 12), evil women use seductive speech.

The evil woman turns away from the right path (see v. 13).

**companion.** Her husband.

**covenant of her God.** If the “forbidden woman” is a non-Israelite (v. 16 note), “covenant” may refer to a marriage witnessed by some foreign god. More likely, the woman is an Israelite who transgresses the requirements of the covenant given at Sinai, particularly the commandment against adultery (Ex. 20:14).

In OT Wisdom Literature, life is not mere existence but a way characterized by true relationships that conform to God’s design. Death is not only the end of physical life but an irreversible descent into the disorder of moral perversity (cf. 5:23, where “dies” is parallel with “led astray”).
This note of finality highlights the seriousness of breaching standards that are not merely social customs but creation ordinances of God.
Deliverance from” evil people creates space for walking in the way of good people.

The promise of land was a basic part of the covenant God made with Abraham, Moses, and the people (Gen. 13:15 and note; Ex. 20:12; Deut. 1:8; 26:1–9). These promises foreshadow the promise of eternal life (Hb. 11:16) and the meek’s inheriting the earth (Matt. 5:5). The conditional aspect of the covenant is reflected here (Gen. 17:2 note)—the upright and the wise inherit the land, but the wicked are removed (Deut. 28).

These verses are the third instruction in the first collection and focus on one’s relationship with God by holding on to the teaching (vv. 1–4), centering on the Lord (vv. 5–10), and accepting God’s discipline (vv. 11, 12). The repetition of “my son” in vv. 1, 11 marks the boundaries of the section, and the consistent use of couplets evidences the internal unity.

**3:1–4** The first two couplets focus on holding on to the teaching (“do not forget,” keep,” “let not ... forsake,” “bind,” and “write”), which advances the acceptance of the teaching in 2:1.

**3:1 teaching.** See note on 1:8.

**commandments.** This word is also found in the law. As is typical of the parallel phrases of Hebrew poetry, the second half of the verse repeats the idea of the first half, clarifying it or expanding on it. Essentially, this verse means to memorize the commands and then put them into practice.

Refers to quantity of life.

**years of life.** Refers to quality of life. The normal expectation is that wisdom will lead to a long, prosperous life, which is the blessing of God (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 6:1–3).

**peace.** Heb. _shalom._ The term denotes general well-being, a harmony of relationships, wholeness, and health (v. 8). In the OT, the blessings of God are seen primarily in terms of this present life. It was not easy to reconcile this perspective with the suffering of the righteous or the prosperity of the wicked. The revelation that would come with Christ, especially in His resurrection from the dead, was still far in the future.

Metonyms for the teaching and commandments of v. 1, since it is the latter that are characteristically bound and written (6:20, 21; 7:2, 3; Deut. 6:8). The teachings and commandments in Proverbs are characterized by love and faithfulness.
Reputation is the sense (text note). Jesus lived this out, as it is written, “Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52).

LORD**.** Rely entirely upon the Lord’s Word and promises as revealed through the sage (2:6; 16:20). See note on 1:7.

**lean ... understanding.** The text warns against relying exclusively on one’s own understanding, but does not prohibit using it.

This is the practical expression of the mind that submits to God and knows Him.

**he will make straight your paths.** The straight path is the path of the righteous (2:20) that leads to life (12:28) and is to be contrasted with the crooked path (2:15) that leads to death (2:19). The straight path is also the level path (15:19); both are metaphors for freedom from obstacles (see 3:23; 4:12).
Summarizes the idea that the human mind with its intellect and reason is independently capable of reaching a true understanding of reality, without dependence upon God’s revelation.

Lit. “navel” (text note), which may be a figure of speech where a part stands for the whole, and thus refers to the outer body. Since one cannot see the bones, they may serve as a figure for the inner person. Together, “flesh” and “bones” stand for the whole person.

To esteem one as having importance.

**wealth ... firstfruits.** The poet moves from the general (material wealth) to the specific (the best part of one’s wealth). Honoring God with the right use of material things expresses gratitude for His favor and recognizes that He controls the natural order and its processes.

The three basic products for the ancient Israelite farmer were grain, wine, and oil (Deut. 11:14; 12:17; Hos. 2:8; Joel 2:24). Barns full of grain and vats full of wine symbolize prosperity on all levels.

The repetition of “my son” (3:1) signals the end of this instructional poem.

**discipline.** Although the instruction of God will require chastisement, this correction is not calculated to harm or anger His children. But because chastisement is difficult, specific encouragement not to rebel against it is necessary.
Discipline is the expression of the Father’s love for His children. Heb. 12:3–11 explains that God’s correction is better than that of an earthly father; cf. Luke 11:11–13.

Another wisdom poem. This one focuses on the benefits of wisdom, both the blessings of wisdom (vv. 13–18) and its effectiveness (vv. 19, 20).

**3:13–18** The repetition of “blessed” in vv. 13 and 18 marks the beginning and end of this section, and it focuses attention on the main theme: the blessings of wisdom.

**3:13 Blessed.** The Hb. word _ashrey_, used almost exclusively in the Wisdom Literature, refers to well-being in every area of life (see Ps. 112). The one who finds wisdom, like the one who meditates on God’s instruction (Ps. 1), is blessed.
Job 28 describes wisdom as a treasure. Ps. 19:10 refers specifically to the revealed law., 15
See v. 2 and notes. One of the reasons that wisdom is better than wealth is that wisdom brings wealth as well as long life and honor., 17

Probably not a specific allusion to the tree of life in Gen. 2:9, though the author would have known of it. In the literature of the time, the flourishing tree was a common figure for continuing blessings. The metaphor is used again in 11:30; 13:12; 15:4. More important is the theme of “life” in Proverbs. “Life” in the Bible is essentially linked to our relationship with God. Disruption of the proper relationship with God, the source of life, leads to death (Gen. 2:17). Wisdom is concerned with proper relationships with God, other people, and nature.

These verses are linked to vv. 13–18 by the repetition of “wisdom” and “understanding” in vv. 13 and 19 and focus on the effectiveness of wisdom.

**3:19 by wisdom ... by understanding.** God’s wisdom is so effective that it was used to create earth and heaven.

**earth ... heavens.** God’s wisdom produced the well-ordered world of earth beneath and heaven above, implying also all creation between earth and heaven.

**3:20 deeps broke open ... clouds drop the dew.** The word translated “broke open” is the same word used in Gen. 7:11 for God’s opening the terrestrial source of water. Since “dew” does not drop from clouds, the Hb. word refers here, as in a few other places, to rain. Thus God provides water from the terrestrial and celestial sources. The point of vv. 19, 20 is that since God’s wisdom created such a well-ordered world for Him, God’s wisdom can surely create a well-ordered world in our lives.

An instructional poem that focuses on wisdom and relating to our neighbor: wisdom’s benefits (vv. 21–24), the good neighbor (vv. 25–32), and wisdom’s outcomes (vv. 33–35).

**3:21–24** These verses focus on the need to hold on to wisdom (v. 21) and the benefits that will result (vv. 22–24).

**3:21** See notes on v. 1 and 1:4.

Here as elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the word for “soul” refers to the whole person.

**adornment.** The Hb. word is a common term for “favor.” Wisdom brings “favor ... in the sight of God and man” (3:4).
See note on 3:6.
**not be afraid.** Part of wisdom is the avoidance of life-threatening situations, not by refusing to face danger when necessary but by pursuing right relationships and an orderly existence.

verse_quote: sudden terror ... ruin of the wicked.
note: In context, the sense seems to be the ruin that might be brought about by a wicked neighbor.
The Lord will protect the righteous from a wicked neighbor.
Contains a series of commandments (“Do not”) about relating to our neighbor, the first and the last containing explanatory clauses (“for”).
Devious people are alienated from God, but those who are righteous enjoy intimacy with the Lord.

The commands of vv. 25–32 have come to an end, and this instructional poem ends by spelling out the two outcomes of one’s choices in life.

**3:33** Here the typical proverbial contrast between the righteous and the wicked (cf. 10:2, 3, 6, 7, 11, 16) is related to God’s blessings and curses. This parallels the covenant theology of Deuteronomy, in which faithfulness is rewarded by the blessings of God (Deut. 11:26–29; 28:1–19).

verse_quote: to the humble he gives favor.
note: See James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5.

These verses are wisdom passed down from a grandfather to his son and then to his grandson, focusing on the need to embrace wisdom.

**4:1 sons.** The first of four occurrences of “sons” in place of the usual “son” (see 5:7; 7:24; 8:32). The shift is probably an indicator of the fact that Proverbs is a compilation of various collections of wisdom teaching.
Or “learning,” as in 1:5. The Hb. term emphasizes the receptive activity of the learner; it stems from the same root of the verb translated “receive” in 1:3.

The wise continue the tradition of wisdom by passing on to succeeding generations the wisdom they learned from their parents. Ps. 78 is a wisdom psalm that has this same transgenerational approach to the teaching of wisdom. Age and experience are not absolute authorities, but they are important and must be highly regarded (Lev. 19:32).

**4:4 live.** See notes on 2:18 and 3:2.

Note the parallel structure in this verse, where the second line says almost the same as the first yet with some development of thought. “Do not forsake” becomes the positive injunction to “love.” Wisdom is far more than an accumulation of facts. It involves trust and commitment.

This embrace of the need for wisdom goes hand in hand with the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (1:7), for it is only in fearing God that we realize our need for wisdom.

**whatever you get.** Jesus used a similar saying about how one should seek the kingdom of God (Matt. 13:45, 46).
One benefit of wisdom is that wisdom brings other benefits. See note on 1:9.

These verses, marked out at the beginning by “Hear, my son” (see 4:1, 20), focus on wisdom and the two ways: the way of wisdom (vv. 10–13, 18) and the way of the wicked (vv. 14–17, 19).

**4:10 accept.** See 1:3.

**years ... many.** See note on 3:2.

verse_quote: way of wisdom ... paths of uprightness.
note: The metaphor of life as a way or a path is common in Israelite wisdom. Wisdom and uprightness go together, showing the moral side of wisdom, as do folly and wickedness (10:18; 14:16; 24:9).
The path of wisdom is the straight path (3:6 note).
Life cannot exist without wisdom. In the NT, Christ is called our wisdom (1 Cor. 1:30) and our life (Col. 3:4).

Wisdom typically contrasts opposing ways and ideas (esp. in the concise proverbs of chs. 10–22). This teaching device accentuates the path of wisdom by opposing various aspects of it to the path of folly and evil. Here vv. 11–13 contrast with vv. 14–17, and v. 18 with v. 19.
Evil is like an addictive drug. Those who embrace it find that without their daily dose they are unable to sleep.
Eating and drinking image the joy and satisfaction of life elsewhere (Eccl. 2:4 note), but the wicked pervert these blessings.
These verses use imagery of an ever-increasing light to characterize righteousness and an impenetrable gloom for wickedness (John 8:12; Eph. 5:8–13)., 19

Builds on the previous section and culminates in a call to stay on the right path.

**4:20 my son.** Typical at the beginning of a new section.

**be attentive ... incline your ear.** The language of submission to God’s instruction (2:2 note).
The seat of reason and the will (2:2 note).
Wholeness and soundness that include the body (3:8).
Our thoughts shape the way we speak and live. See Matt. 12:35; Mark 7:21; Rom. 2:29.
“Crooked” and “devious” characterize the speech of the wicked (2:12, 16) as well as their general lifestyle (2:15). What is on one’s lips is a reflection of one’s life.
Keeping the eyes straight on the path of wisdom is the responsibility of the one who trusts the Lord to make the path straight (3:6).
See note on 4:12.
See Deut. 5:32.

These verses focus on wisdom and two women, an adulteress and one’s wife: an instruction to stay away from the forbidden woman (vv. 1–6), a second instruction to stay away from her (vv. 7–14), an instruction to embrace one’s wife (vv. 15–19), and a concluding instruction to stay away from the forbidden woman (vv. 20–23). The repetition of “forbidden woman” in vv. 3, 20 serves to tie these sections together as a unit. Wisdom urges us to avoid the life-destroying adulteress and to find sexual and emotional satisfaction in the bonds of marriage.

**5:1–6** Describes the character of the forbidden woman. On the surface she is sweetness and light, but underneath is the bitter taste of death.

**5:1 be attentive ... incline your ear.** The language of submission to God’s instruction (4:20 note).
The sense seems to be that his lips should be involved with holding on to knowledge by means of the recitation of Scripture rather than being involved with “the lips of a forbidden woman” (5:3).

While her lips are associated with speech in the next line, it is hard not to hear a reference to her seductive kiss as well. In contrast with v. 2, the seducer begins with deceptive words of charm. Cf. the sweetness of true love in Song 4:11.

The phrase speaks of the end result for one who lets himself be seduced.

**bitter as wormwood.** A plant especially bitter to the taste, wormwood is used as a metaphor for the experience of affliction (Deut. 29:18).

**two-edged sword.** The smoothness of her words is deceptive (v. 3), and the liaison leads only to injury.

Not merely a matter of an early demise brought about by dissolute living, death in this context is all that does not promote life as defined by God.

**Sheol.** The place of the dead, the grave. Disorderly life leads to physical death. See note on Is. 14:9–11.
The moral censure here is inseparable from the wisdom idea that folly and wickedness involve a rejection of God’s order and plan for things.
These verses provide a more detailed description of the results of immorality and the price it exacts.
The wise will make a conscious choice to avoid any contact with immorality and keep out of the way of temptation.

Both should be gained through wisdom (3:16), not lost through folly.

**the merciless.** Perhaps the outraged husband of the adulteress (6:34, 35).
This verse may refer literally to the high cost of keeping a mistress (a “foreigner”). More likely, the warning is that immorality takes away wealth and strength.
Both should find healing through wisdom (3:7, 8), not demise through folly.
Sexual immorality epitomizes the way of folly that rejects the discipline of wise instruction., 13
In view here is either public disgrace or punishment by the covenant community.

These verses are similar to the love poetry of the Song of Solomon.

These verses consist mainly of single-sentence proverbs and are intended to teach those who embrace wisdom how to live out that wisdom in all of life. The unity of the section is marked by the heading in 10:1, “The proverbs of Solomon”; the shift to “the words of the wise” in 22:17; and the fact that the section contains 375 proverbs, the numerical equivalent to Solomon’s name in Hebrew.

There is no evidence that these are a form of wisdom literature from a different time than the longer instructions of chs. 1–9. They are simply different forms and function in different ways. Aphorisms are often stated without qualifications; they are thus often misinterpreted as promises rather than proverbs.

The wisdom of Proverbs presupposes and builds upon the special revelation of God in the Mosaic law (1:8 note). The Hebrew sages assumed that, given human intelligence and the gift of God’s wisdom in His self-revelation, God’s people can discern the order and relationships that make for a meaningful and productive life. The wisdom of Proverbs is the fruit of experience and reflection, stressing the need to think through and apply human knowledge and the Word of God to all affairs of life in a responsible way.

As is sometimes the case in the Bible, the chapter divisions are rather arbitrary and do not aid the analysis of the text. The individual sentences can be classified according to their literary structures and themes. Chapters 10–15 consist mainly of contrasts between opposites, as indicated by the conjunction “but” introducing the second line of most of these proverbs. This common literary device uses contrasting pairs such as “righteous” vs. “wicked” and “wise” vs. “fool.” Occasional grouping of sentences according to theme and form is evident in the book, a method that aids memorization but does not assist the interpretation of the mostly independent sayings. Each sentence has its own social setting and special aim. Much like folk sayings in other societies, some of the sayings have been separated from their contexts in order to provide concise, practical guidelines for living.

The metaphor is curiously mixed. The result of righteousness is life. See 3:18 and note; 13:12; 15:4.

Lit. “loving discipline, loving knowledge.” The form of this proverb, like 13:3 and 14:2, groups things that belong together without explicitly stating the relationship. See 10:25 and note.

**to be lowly.** A person of no social standing or reputation.

**righteous.** See note on 8:18.

The principle of rewards, expressed, e.g. in v. 21, is focused on wise speech. Such speech creates good relationships and shows care for the life-enhancing order of things. Its rewards are as tangible as those of physical labor.
The fool thinks he knows better than others. The wise person is humble enough to learn from the experience of others and has the ability to discern good counsel (v. 1).
Self-control is characteristic of the wise. The fool reacts too strongly and too soon, destroying relationships. The wise person leaves the way open for reconciliation.
At first glance, this proverb expresses what should be self-evident, but it effectively illustrates the inevitable relationship between character and deeds (v. 5 note).

This basic condition of the righteous refers both to natural calamity and the judgment of God. See note on 10:22.
The Lord’s self-revealed character and attitudes provide a strong motive for truth.

Not out of selfishness but so that he does not parade his knowledge. Wisdom knows when to keep silent and when to speak (26:4, 5; Eccl. 3:7; James 3:17, 18).

**no death.** Hb. “not death.” See note on 3:2.

Having control over one’s speech so that what is said is carefully considered for its possible effects.

–**33** A collection of somewhat longer wisdom poems, including a number of numerical says. The unity of this collection is marked by the title in 30:1, “The words of Agur,” and the title of the following collection in 31:1, “The words of King Lemuel.”

**30:1** –**6** These verses are a poem that contrasts the limits of human wisdom with the reliability of divine revelation.

**30:1 Agur son of Jakeh.** His identity is unknown, but many consider him to be a foreigner. See note on 22:17–24:22 and Introduction: Author.

**The oracle.** It is possible that the Hb. word is a place name, “Massa” (also in 31:1), and that both Agur and Lemuel were Ishmaelites from Massa, thought to be in Arabia (Gen. 25:14).

**I am weary ... worn out.** These lines are difficult; see text note.

This statement is not mere modesty or humility but a recognition of the mystery of the being and ways of God such as is found in Job and Ecclesiastes. The writer is acutely conscious of the bounds of human knowledge and wisdom. God is not an object for our investigation or speculation but the infinite and personal creator in whom we must trust. There may be a note of irony in the profession of ignorance here, but v. 4 indicates the meaning., 3

These questions express the conviction that knowledge based solely on observation of creation can never fully comprehend God. In Job 28, the same point is made, as it is in the course of God’s answer to Job in 38:1–40:2.

With these words, Agur gives and assessment of God’s Word within the framework of Israel’s law and prophetic writings. He quotes Ps. 18:30 and echoes Deut. 4:2. The full knowledge of God comes through special revelation and is received by faith (1:7 note).

**30:5 proves true.** Tried and found to be utterly reliable.

**30:6 Do not add to his words.** To add to God’s words is to sit in judgment on them and to find them wanting by human standards. This shifts the basis of knowledge and truth from God to ourselves. This pride of the creature is a wellspring of sin (Gen. 2:9 note).

–**9** These verses are a discrete unit that contains advice to the king. Wisdom was a royal enterprise in the ancient world; see note on 1:1.

**31:1 The words of King Lemuel.** While these are the “words of King Lemuel,” he is obviously not the author, since he was taught them by his mother. Similarly, “the Proverbs of Solomon” (1:1) do not all necessarily come directly from Solomon, but many of them would have been taught to him and left for him to pass on. Lemuel was not an Israelite king; see note on 30:1. The nature of this section (vv. 1–9) suggests an Egyptian or perhaps a Bab­ylonian origin. Its intention is apparently vocational, the equipping of the ruler for his task. The form is similar to the instructions of chs. 1–9 (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). In this case, the teaching is given by the mother (1:8; 4:1, 3). While the father may have been the principal teacher of the children, godly women also took that role (cf. 14:1 note), and there were in Israel noteworthy wise women (2 Sam. 14:2; 20:16).

**strong drink.** This translation may lead the reader to think of distilled beverages such as whiskey, but there is no evidence that the ancients knew the distillation process. They did understand fermentation, and ancient beer recipes have been discovered. So when paired with “wine,” beer is in all likelihood the meaning.

The king’s task is to uphold righteousness in society. In Israel, this task was viewed in the context of the covenant with the Lord (Deut. 17:14–20)., 9

Some include vv. 10–31 in the words of King Lemuel, but they are better taken as a concluding poem for the entire book. This section, which has no title, matches the opening section, 1:8–9:18, which also has no title. In 1:8–9:18, two women vie for the heart of the young man. In 31:10–31 only one woman remains, Wisdom. This section is primarily a final portrayal of Lady Wisdom in all her beauty. Secondarily, it is a poem extolling the virtues of a wife who exemplifies the principles of wisdom, both practically and spiritually. The sequence of virtues is governed more by the demands of the acrostic (the first word in each verse beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet) than by logic. Yet the overall effect is of a coherent description of a woman beautified by her virtues of practical wisdom and charity. That the household described is well-to-do underscores the rewards of wisdom.

**31:10 excellent wife.** The Hb. word translated “excellent” has connotations of power (see v. 17) and is used in military contexts. Ruth is the only woman given this appellation (Ruth 3:11; see Prov. 12:4). It is perhaps not coincidental that in the order of the Hebrew Bible the book of Ruth follows the book of Proverbs.

LORD**.** Up to this point, the poem concentrates on practical wisdom. Now the basis of all true wisdom is emphasized, as the book of Proverbs ends where it begins: the fear of the Lord. Observation of the created order can provide some wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom. 1:20–23), but only the self-revelation of the Creator enables us to know and appreciate the God-centered meaning of reality. True wisdom is seen as the life lived in wholehearted obedience to God’s revelation in His Word and world, which is “the fear of the Lord” (1:7 and note). This trust is the foundation and continuing path of wisdom for both men and women as it brings us to final perfection in Christ., 31
